section.title: The Demoniac, Jairus, and the Bleeding Woman
section.sectionRationale: Three unforgettable rescues show Jesus' authority reaching to the furthest extremities of human ruin. He frees a man enslaved by a legion of demons among the tombs, heals a woman drained by twelve years of bleeding, and raises a synagogue leader's dead daughter. Demons, chronic defilement, and death itself all yield to His word and His touch.
section.thesis: Jesus is Lord over the demonic, the defiling, and the dead, meeting the most hopeless cases, the raging outcast, the unclean and impoverished woman, and a lifeless child, with a power and mercy that restore them whole, and He calls for faith rather than fear.
section.frameNote: Three rescues, with the last two interwoven: the Gerasene demoniac set free; the bleeding woman healed by touching Jesus' cloak; and the raising of Jairus's daughter.

units.label: The Gerasene demoniac set free
units.note: Legion cast out, the man restored

verses.text: On the other side of the sea, they arrived in the region of the Gerasenes.
As soon as Jesus got out of the boat, He was met by a man with an unclean spirit, who was coming from the tombs.
This man had been living in the tombs and could no longer be restrained, even with chains.
Though he was often bound with chains and shackles, he had broken the chains and shattered the shackles. Now there was no one with the strength to subdue him.
Night and day in the tombs and in the mountains he kept crying out and cutting himself with stones.
When the man saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and fell on his knees before Him.
And he shouted in a loud voice, “What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg You before God not to torture me!”
For Jesus had already declared, “Come out of this man, you unclean spirit!”
“What is your name?” Jesus asked. “My name is {{legion|Legion}},” he replied, “for we are many.”
And he begged Jesus repeatedly not to send them out of that region.
There on the nearby hillside a large herd of pigs was feeding.
So the demons begged Jesus, “Send us to the pigs, so that we may enter them.”
He gave them permission, and the unclean spirits came out and went into the pigs, and the herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the water.
Those tending the pigs ran off and reported this in the town and countryside, and the people went out to see what had happened.
When they came to Jesus, they saw the man who had been possessed by the legion of demons sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.
Those who had seen it described what had happened to the demon-possessed man and also to the pigs.
And the people began to beg Jesus to leave their region.
As He was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed by the demons begged to go with Him.
But Jesus would not allow him. “Go home to your own people,” He said, “and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.”
So the man went away and began to proclaim throughout the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him. And everyone was amazed.

units.label: The bleeding woman healed
units.note: if only I touch His garments

verses.text: When Jesus had again crossed by boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around Him beside the sea.
A synagogue leader named Jairus arrived, and seeing Jesus, he fell at His feet
and pleaded with Him urgently, “My little daughter is near death. Please come and place Your hands on her, so that she will be healed and live.”
So Jesus went with him, and a large crowd followed and pressed around Him.
And a woman was there who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years.
She had borne much agony under the care of many physicians and had spent all she had, but to no avail. Instead, her condition had only grown worse.
When the woman heard about Jesus, she came up through the crowd behind Him and touched His cloak.
For she kept saying, “If only I touch His garments, I will be {{sozo|healed}}.”
Immediately her bleeding stopped, and she sensed in her body that she was healed of her affliction.
At once Jesus was aware that power had gone out from Him. Turning to the crowd, He asked, “Who touched My garments?”
His disciples answered, “You can see the crowd pressing in on You, and yet You ask, ‘Who touched Me?’”
But He kept looking around to see who had done this.
Then the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before Him trembling in fear, and she told Him the whole truth.
“Daughter,” said Jesus, “your {{pistis|faith}} has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.”

units.label: The raising of Jairus's daughter
units.note: little girl, I say to you, get up

verses.text: While He was still speaking, messengers from the house of Jairus arrived and said, “Your daughter is dead; why bother the Teacher anymore?”
But Jesus overheard their conversation and said to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just {{pisteuo|believe}}.”
And He did not allow anyone to accompany Him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James.
When they arrived at the house of the synagogue leader, Jesus saw the commotion and the people weeping and wailing loudly.
He went inside and asked, “Why all this commotion and weeping? The child is not dead, but asleep.”
And they laughed at Him. After He had put them all outside, He took the child’s father and mother and His own companions, and went in to see the child.
Taking her by the hand, Jesus said, “{{talitha|Talitha koum}}!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!”
Immediately the girl got up and began to walk around (she was twelve years old). And at once they were utterly astounded.
Then Jesus gave strict orders that no one should know about this, and He told them to give her something to eat.

legion.gloss: Legion, a Latin loanword for a Roman army division of up to six thousand soldiers. The demons name themselves Legion because they are many; the military term conveys the sheer force enslaving the man, and its utter powerlessness before Jesus, who dismisses the whole host with a word.

sozo.gloss: To save, rescue, heal, make whole. The same verb covers bodily healing and eternal salvation. The woman believes touching Jesus' garments will make her well, and Jesus tells her that her faith has saved her, so her healing becomes a picture of the fuller rescue faith receives.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust. It was not the magic of the cloak but the woman's faith that laid hold of Jesus' power; He says her faith has saved her. Faith reaches out to Christ in the crowd of many who merely press against Him, and it receives what He freely gives.

pisteuo.gloss: To believe, trust. As the news of death arrives, Jesus tells Jairus only do not be afraid, just believe. Faith is set against fear; Jairus is called to keep trusting Jesus even past the point where death seems to end all hope.

talitha.gloss: Little girl, get up, the Aramaic words Jesus actually spoke, preserved by Mark and then translated for his readers. The tender, homely command shows Jesus speaking to the dead child as gently as a parent waking a sleeper, and death obeys.

basic.context: Mark shows Jesus overpowering three enemies. First, across the lake, a man tormented by a legion of demons lives naked among the tombs, uncontrollable, until Jesus casts the demons out into a herd of pigs and the man is found clothed and sane. The frightened locals ask Jesus to leave, but the freed man goes to tell everyone what the Lord has done. Back across the water, a synagogue leader named Jairus begs Jesus to heal his dying daughter. On the way, a woman who has bled for twelve years touches Jesus' cloak and is instantly healed; Jesus stops to honour her faith. Then news comes that the girl has died, but Jesus goes on, takes her by the hand, and raises her with a word.
basic.hermeneutics: These are demonstrations of who Jesus is: Lord over demons, disease, and death. Notice the recurring themes of faith versus fear and of Jesus touching the unclean, the demoniac, the bleeding woman, the corpse, without being defiled; instead He makes them whole. The interwoven stories of Jairus and the woman invite comparison: both involve twelve years, both need desperate faith.
basic.originalLanguages: The demons call themselves legion, an army, yet flee at a word. The woman is sure that touching Jesus will make her sozo, saved or healed, and Jesus credits her pistis, faith. To Jairus He says simply pisteuo, believe. And He raises the girl with the Aramaic talitha koum, little girl, get up.
basic.typology: Jesus touching the unclean and the dead without contracting defilement reverses the flow of the law: holiness overcomes uncleanness. His raising of the girl is a foretaste of His own resurrection and of the general resurrection He guarantees.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Son of the Most High God, as the demon confesses. He commands demons, heals the incurable, and raises the dead. Every scene answers Mark's question, who is this, with the same reply: the Lord of life.
basic.god: God's power and mercy meet the most hopeless cases. The Lord has done great things and shown mercy, as Jesus tells the freed man to report. God calls for faith in the face of fear and even death.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 65 pictures those who dwell among tombs. Leviticus 15 gives the law of the bleeding woman's uncleanness. John 11 records the raising of Lazarus, a fuller sign of the same power.
basic.oneStory: The kingdom that comes hidden as seed also comes with power to reclaim what evil, sickness, and death have stolen. Jesus frees the enslaved, cleanses the defiled, and raises the dead, previews of the final rescue when the King will banish every demon, wipe away every tear, and raise His people to life that never ends.

context.literary:
Mark 5 follows the storm of 4:35-41 without a break, and the two chapters should be read as one long crossing. The Lord who stilled the wind and sea steps out of the boat in 5:2 and meets the next force that seems beyond control. The narrative gives three escalating encounters, each against a worse enemy: a legion of demons, a chronic disease, and death itself. Each time the power of Jesus is shown to be more than enough.

The structure is a sandwich, one of Mark's favourite devices. The story of Jairus opens at 5:21-24, is interrupted by the woman with bleeding in 5:25-34, and resumes with the news of the girl's death in 5:35-43. The interruption is not a delay but a commentary. While Jesus is on His way to a dying girl, He stops for someone no one notices, and that stop is what brings the messengers with their terrible news. The two stories are joined by twelve years: the woman had been ill for twelve years and the girl was twelve, 5:25 and 5:42. Jairus has a name and a position; the woman has neither. He approaches openly and falls at Jesus' feet; she comes from behind in secret and, once caught, falls trembling at His feet too. Mark joins the highest and lowest of the community under the same Lord.

The demoniac story, 5:1-20, is the longest single miracle account in Mark, and its details are full of vivid action, chains, shackles, stones, tombs, a herd, a cliff. It is built as a series of reversals: the man who could not be bound is brought to sit still, the one who lived among the dead is found 'clothed and in his right mind,' the one begging not to be tormented is the one who is delivered, and the crowd who were afraid of the demoniac are now afraid of the healed man. The one who begged Jesus not to send the demons out of the region is balanced by the people who beg Jesus to leave it.

Finally, the whole chapter sits between two statements of fear. At 4:41 the disciples fear greatly, and at 5:15 and 5:33 and 5:36 the word 'fear' keeps returning. Jesus' answer to Jairus, 'Do not be afraid; just believe,' sums up the movement of the entire section.
context.historical:
The place is the east side of the Sea of Galilee, outside Jewish Galilee. The name is hard to fix, since the manuscripts of the Gospels give Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes for the district. The BSB reads Gerasenes. Whatever the town, it is clear that Jesus has crossed into largely Gentile land, linked to the Decapolis, a group of ten cities with a Greek character east and south of the lake, as 5:20 says. The detail of a large herd of pigs makes the point. Pigs were unclean to Jews, Leviticus 11:7, and keeping a herd of two thousand tells us who lived here. The Gentile mission, which looks so far off in Mark, has already begun in a small way.

Tombs were a place of uncleanness. Touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days, Numbers 19:11, and so burial caves outside towns were avoided by the pure. They were also, in the imagination of the day, a place where unclean spirits lived. Isaiah 65:4 describes a rebellious people 'sitting among the graves' and eating the meat of pigs, and the man in Mark 5 is a living picture of that uncleanness. The word 'Legion' is a Latin military term borrowed into Greek, the name of the Roman army's largest unit, which at full strength numbered several thousand men. For a people who lived under Roman occupation, it carried a charge. Some have noted a political overtone in the army that drowns in the sea, but Mark does not press it, so we should not.

The law of Leviticus 15:25-30 treats a woman with a long-lasting flow of blood as unclean for as long as it continued, and anything she sat on or touched became unclean as well. After twelve years she had been shut out of ordinary worship and probably of ordinary family life. Mark also notes that she had 'spent all she had' on physicians and grown worse. Her touching a stranger in a crowd was a risk, and her coming forward, 'trembling in fear,' reflects that.

Jairus was one of the leaders responsible for the synagogue's affairs, and he came out in public at the risk of his standing, since the leaders were increasingly hostile, 3:6. Mourning in that world was loud and quick: relatives, and often hired mourners and flute players, began wailing as soon as a death was known, which is why the house is already in commotion in verse 38. Burial normally followed the same day.
context.canonical:
The strongest echoes in the demoniac story come from the sea. The drowning of the herd recalls the way Pharaoh's army was swept into the sea, Exodus 14:26-28 and 15:4-5, and Psalm 107 pairs deliverance from chains and darkness in verses 10 to 16 with deliverance from the storm in verses 23 to 30. In Mark 4 and 5 the Lord does both in order: first the sea, then the chains. Leviathan and the dragon of the sea, whom God is said to crush in Psalm 74:13-14 and to slay in Isaiah 27:1, stand in the background as images of the forces that the sea represents.

Isaiah 65:1-5 is the nearest Old Testament picture of the man's state: a people who sit among graves and eat pig's meat, and whom the LORD still reaches out to with open hands. The text starts with 'I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me.' Mark 5 shows the answer: a man in the very condition Isaiah describes is found by the one he did not seek.

The woman's story has to be read with Leviticus 15:25-30, which defines her uncleanness. Her story reverses what the law expected. In the law the unclean person makes what she touches unclean, but here the clean power of Jesus makes her clean. The prophets hoped for such cleansing, as in Ezekiel 36:25-27, where God promises to sprinkle clean water and give a new heart and spirit.

The raising of the girl stands in a line with two earlier raisings by prophets: Elijah's raising of the widow's son in 1 Kings 17:21-23, and Elisha's raising of the Shunammite's son in 2 Kings 4:32-37. In each case the prophet prayed and stretched himself over the child. Jesus uses neither prayer nor ritual, only a word and a hand. Later Scripture gives the hope behind it: the dead will live, Isaiah 26:19, and many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, Daniel 12:2. The New Testament carries the story forward in the raising of the widow's son at Nain, Luke 7:11-17, and of Lazarus, John 11:38-44, until it reaches Christ's own resurrection, and the word in verse 41, 'get up,' is the verb that the New Testament uses for His rising.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark means this chapter to answer a question posed at its start. At 4:41 the disciples asked who this was. Chapter 5 gives the answer in three acts, each larger than the last: He rules over spirits, over illness and over death. Nothing that terrifies people is outside His reach. The first readers, living in a world with hostile powers, chronic illness and early death, were meant to feel that the one they followed was greater than any of them.

Mark also shows the kind of response that He looks for. The demons recognised Him and could not resist; the crowd feared Him and asked Him to leave; the woman reached for Him in need; Jairus risked his reputation; and the man who was freed wanted to follow Him. The one who is told to stay and speak is sent as the first witness among the Gentiles. The chapter holds up both faith in need and obedience in sending.

Mark's readers would also have seen that the unclean are not left outside. Jesus goes to the tombs, speaks to the woman whom the law excluded and takes a dead child by the hand. The point is not that He ignores purity, but that He brings a cleansing power greater than the uncleanness. For Gentile readers, and for any who feared that their past or their condition cut them off, this is the heart of the good news.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what Jesus did on one journey across the lake. It does not promise that every sick person will be healed or every dead child raised. Mark reports these acts as signs of who Jesus is and of the kingdom He brings, not as a guarantee about our own circumstances. We would misuse the story if we turned it into a formula for health.

Nor does the chapter command touching bleeding people or visiting tombs. What Jesus does with the law of uncleanness is a statement about His own person, the holy One who cleanses what He touches, not a general instruction to ignore Moses' rules for others. The law's purity code had its purpose in teaching Israel about God's holiness, and Mark's point is that its goal is reached in Him.

What is plainly prescribed is in Jesus' words. To the freed man: 'Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you.' To the woman: 'Go in peace.' To Jairus: 'Do not be afraid; just believe.' These are spoken to particular people, but the pattern is open to everyone: those who have received mercy are to tell of it, those who have been healed may go in peace, and those facing the worst are asked to go on trusting. The man's commission to witness at home is the most widely applicable, since most believers are sent to their own neighbours first.

debates.question: Why did Jesus allow the demons to enter the pigs and destroy the herd?

views.label: A visible proof of real deliverance
views.case: The herd's rush into the sea is public, undeniable evidence that the demons truly left the man, and it shows the destructive nature of the forces that had been tearing at him. They end by destroying what they enter.

views.label: The worth of one person over property
views.case: A man made in God's image is worth far more than two thousand animals, and the townspeople's alarm over the pigs shows where their values lay. The loss of unclean animals in Gentile territory is a cheap price for a restored man.

views.label: A sign of judgment on unclean powers
views.case: The demons asked to go into the pigs and ended in the sea, the traditional place of the doom of God's enemies. Some read the scene against the drowning of Pharaoh's army, as a sign that the powers that held people captive are going to destruction.

debates.bearing: Each reading agrees that the deliverance was real and complete and that the person is worth more than any herd. The text does not explain more than it says, and we should not claim to know.

debates.question: Was the girl really dead, or only in a deep sleep?

views.label: She was truly dead and raised
views.case: The messengers say 'Your daughter is dead,' the mourners are already wailing, and the crowd's laughter shows they were sure of it. Luke adds that they laughed 'knowing that she was dead,' Luke 8:53. Jesus' 'asleep' is a way of describing death as temporary in His hands, as with Lazarus in John 11:11-14, where He says Lazarus is asleep and then plainly says he is dead.

views.label: She was in a coma or a trance
views.case: Some who doubt miracles take Jesus' words, 'The child is not dead, but asleep,' literally and suppose she was unconscious. This view has to explain why every witness thought she was dead and why Mark and the other Gospels count the event among Jesus' acts of power.

views.label: The sleep language is a statement about God's power
views.case: Jesus' words make a theological claim. In His presence death is as temporary as sleep, which is why the New Testament goes on to speak of believers who have 'fallen asleep,' 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14. The statement does not deny that she was dead but says what her death means before Him.

debates.bearing: The first reading best fits all the details, and the third explains the language. The girl is raised because He who holds life says so, and the text asks for trust, not for analysis.

debates.question: Why does Jesus send the freed man to proclaim, while silencing others?

views.label: Gentile country, where the danger of a political messiah was lower
views.case: In Jewish Galilee the crowds were ready to make Jesus a political king, so He kept His identity quiet. In the Decapolis there was no such expectation, so it was safe for the man to speak. This reading fits Mark's pattern of secrecy.

views.label: The man was a witness to mercy, not to a title
views.case: The man is told to speak of 'how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you,' which is a testimony to mercy and not to Jesus' messianic identity. The silence commands in Mark guard the title, and the man is given leave to tell his story.

views.label: A pointer to the later Gentile mission
views.case: The freed man becomes the first preacher among the Gentiles, ahead of the apostles, and sets the pattern for a mission beyond Israel, Mark 13:10 and 14:9.

debates.bearing: These readings fit together. The silence guarded what was not yet to be understood, and the man's witness to mercy could be told. Both serve Mark's concern for the right time to confess Jesus.

study.originalLanguages:
Begin with the demon's cry in verse 7, 'What do You want with me?' The Greek is an idiom, ti emoi kai soi, literally 'What to me and to you?' It is a way of pushing someone away, and it appears when the widow of Zarephath says it to Elijah, 1 Kings 17:18, and when the demon in the synagogue says it in Mark 1:24. It marks a boundary: we have nothing in common. The title 'Son of the Most High God' uses the word hypsistos, 'Most High,' a title for God often found on Gentile lips, as when Melchizedek blesses Abram in Genesis 14:18-20 and when Nebuchadnezzar speaks in Daniel 4:2. It suits a Gentile setting.

The word 'Legion,' legion, is a Latin loan. A legion's nominal size was some five or six thousand men, though the number would vary, and the herd of about two thousand suggests nothing is to be pressed arithmetically. The man says 'my name is Legion, for we are many,' and slips between singular and plural in the Greek, as Mark's narration also does, 'he' and 'they' alternating. The man is not clearly separate from the forces that hold him.

The man's healed state is described with the verb sophroneo, 'being in his right mind,' a word related to self-control and soundness. It is the opposite of what was said of him before. And 'proclaim,' keryssein, in verse 20 is the word Mark uses for the preaching of the gospel throughout, 1:14 and 1:38. There is a lovely slide in the Greek of verses 19 and 20. Jesus tells the man to tell what 'the Lord,' kyrios, has done, and the man goes and proclaims what 'Jesus,' Iesous, had done. For the man, Jesus is the Lord.

The woman's sickness is described in verse 29 as 'affliction,' mastix, which literally means a whip or scourge, and Mark uses it again in 5:34. Her illness is a scourge. And 'her bleeding stopped' is in the Greek 'the spring of her blood was dried up,' using the word pege, a fountain or spring. The verb for healed in 5:28 and 5:34 is sozo, 'to save,' and it appears in the request of Jairus as well, 5:23, 'so that she will be healed,' sozo, 'and live.' The same verb covers both the healing of the body and the saving of the whole person, and Mark uses one word for the woman and the girl.

Jesus addresses her as 'Daughter,' thygater, a word from the language of the family that He has used in 3:33-35, and Jairus has used it of his own 'little daughter,' thygatrion, a diminutive. The phrase 'Go in peace' translates eis eirenen, which carries the Hebrew shalom, the blessing that Eli gave Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:17.

In verse 36 the command 'Do not be afraid; just believe' uses two present imperatives, 'stop fearing' and 'keep believing,' since the verb is in a form that means continuing action. Faith is asked to carry on through the news of death. In verse 39 'asleep' is katheudo, the same verb used of Jesus Himself in the stern of the boat, 4:38. The sleeper in the storm now calls death a sleep.

Verse 41 preserves the Aramaic words talitha koum. The word talitha means a girl, and koum is an imperative, 'rise.' Mark gives the translation, 'Little girl, I say to you, get up,' using egeiro, a verb that the New Testament uses for being raised from the dead, as at 16:6, 'He has risen.' When He takes her by the hand, the verb is krateo, 'to grasp,' the verb used of the family who wanted to seize Him, 3:21. The same strong grip can seize or raise. Verse 42 uses anistemi, 'to rise,' another resurrection word, and ends with the people 'utterly astounded,' a phrase built from the verb existemi and its noun, which echoes 3:21 where it was said of Jesus that He was 'out of His mind.' People who stood outside themselves in doubt now stand outside themselves in amazement.

typology.type: The drowning of the herd and the sea as the grave of God's enemies
typology.fulfillment: At the Red Sea the army of Pharaoh sank like a stone, Exodus 15:4-5, and the sea became the place where oppressors met their end. In Mark 5 the unclean spirits that held a man captive are swept into the sea, and the man who was in chains is set free to testify. The Gospel does not say outright that Mark wants the Exodus recalled, so this is an echo and not a declared type. The escalation is that the deliverance is not from a human army but from the powers behind the oppression, and what is freed is a single person who is sent to proclaim what the Lord has done, as Israel sang at the sea.

typology.type: The man among the tombs and the unclean people of Isaiah 65
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 65:4 describes people who sit among the graves and eat pig's meat, yet whom God still reaches out to with open hands. The Gerasene man is that picture in flesh, living in the tombs in a land of pigs. Jesus comes to him and he is found clothed and in his right mind. The fulfilment goes beyond what Isaiah showed: the outstretched hands of verse 2 become a person who crosses the sea to find one man. Paul says later that He came to those who did not seek Him, Romans 10:20, and Isaiah's words are applied to the Gentiles.

typology.type: The woman's touch and the reversal of defilement
typology.fulfillment: Under Leviticus 15:25-27 the woman's uncleanness spread to anything she touched, and Jesus would normally have been defiled. The reverse happens: His power flows out and her flow stops. The pattern holds throughout the Gospels, as Jesus touches lepers, Mark 1:41, and corpses, and is not defiled. It looks forward to the cleansing God promised in Ezekiel 36:25-27 and to Hebrews 9:13-14, where the blood of Christ cleanses the conscience. The picture falls short in one respect: the woman's cure is immediate and physical, while the cleansing of Christ's people involves His death.

typology.type: The raising of the girl and the prophets' raisings
typology.fulfillment: Elijah, 1 Kings 17:21-23, and Elisha, 2 Kings 4:32-37, each raised a child by prayer and effort, stretching themselves over the body. Jesus does it with a word and a hand: 'Talitha koum.' The pattern shows Him as greater than the prophets, in line with His claim to be the stronger One. It also previews His own resurrection and that of all who are His, John 5:28-29 and 1 Corinthians 15:20-23. The type is incomplete because the girl was raised to live and die again, while Christ rose to die no more, Romans 6:9.

study.christ:
Mark 5 is arranged so that each scene answers 'Who is this?' with a deeper reply. In the first, the answer comes from the unclean spirit: 'Jesus, Son of the Most High God.' Mark does not suppress it. The enemy knows the identity of Jesus and can do nothing but beg. In the second, the answer is in His body. Power goes out from Him, and the woman is healed by the barest contact with Him. In the third, the answer is in His voice. A word, an Aramaic sentence, returns a child to life. The power that stilled the sea speaks directly to spirits, sickness and death.

Jesus is the one who crosses boundaries and comes out clean. He crosses the sea into Gentile land, goes to the tombs, allows the touch of an unclean woman and takes a corpse by the hand. In each of these He is the one who makes whole. The law's lines of purity are not abolished but fulfilled: where uncleanness would normally spread to Him, holiness spreads from Him. Hebrews says He is a high priest 'who sympathizes with our weaknesses,' Hebrews 4:15, and the woman who trembled with fear was met with 'Daughter.'

He is a Saviour who stops for the individual. On His way to a dying girl, with a crowd pressing, He pauses over one woman whom no one counted. He does not let her slip away quietly with a private cure, but calls her out so that she may hear 'your faith has healed you' and 'go in peace.' He wants the whole person made well and publicly restored, not just the body.

He is the Lord who goes through death. The messengers say it is too late, and Jesus overhears, and answers. For Him it is not too late. His words 'Do not be afraid; just believe' are what He will say all the way to the cross and the empty tomb. The resurrection of the girl is a sign pointing to His own, and He uses the same verb, 'get up,' that will be spoken at the tomb, 'He has risen,' 16:6. The three disciples whom He takes into the house, Peter, James and John, are the same three who will see Him transfigured and who will be with Him in Gethsemane, 9:2 and 14:33. They are given a glimpse of what is coming.

There is a further link in the title the demons use. 'Son of the Most High God' is a confession from a place where no Jew would expect it. It is as if the Gospel wishes to say that the Gentile world, even its darkest part, would come to know who He is. The freed man goes out to proclaim, and the Decapolis hears. By the end of Mark, a Roman centurion will say 'Truly this man was the Son of God,' 15:39.

A word of care. Not every detail is a type. The number of the pigs, the shackles and the cushion are not coded messages, and we should not make the woman's twelve years stand for the twelve tribes unless Mark does. Mark himself links the two stories by the number but does not say what it means. The links above are the ones the Gospel supports: His authority over spirits, disease and death; His holiness that cleanses; and His word that raises.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows of God is that there is nothing too far gone for Him. A man beyond chains, a woman beyond physicians, a girl beyond hope: the Gospel gathers three cases that are humanly hopeless, and each time the answer is not effort but a word or a touch. The doctrine that follows is that God's power is not limited by the size of the problem. It is not a matter of degree, as if God could manage small sicknesses and lacked strength for large ones. Psalm 107 speaks in the same way of those in chains and those in storms, and both are met by the same LORD.

He is a God of mercy, and the phrase comes from the mouth of Jesus Himself. 'Tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and what mercy He has shown you.' Mercy, eleos, is the translation of the Old Testament's chesed, the covenant love that does not let go. The first Gentile witness is to speak of that, and the instruction shows that God's mercy is not an Israelite possession.

He is a God who sees individuals. Jesus stops in a crowd to look for the one who touched Him, and He tells a man to go home to his own people. The Lord does not treat people as interchangeable. The woman could have been left to leave with her cure and her anonymity. Jesus calls her 'Daughter,' placing her within the family, and sends her away in peace. Isaiah 61:1 says the Lord's servant binds up the brokenhearted and frees the captives, and this is what the three stories do.

He is holy in a way that cleanses rather than recoils. Holiness in the law was something like a fire that could spread to what touched it, and uncleanness something to be avoided. In Jesus, God's holiness is stronger than uncleanness and flows out to the unclean. This does not weaken holiness. It shows that it is a living power and not a fragile condition. The God who said 'Be holy, for I am holy' is the God who makes unclean people clean.

He is sovereign over death and the powers. The demons beg for permission and wait for it. That they ask shows the limits God has set for evil, and His permission shows His rule even over it. Death is described by Jesus as a sleep because for Him it is a thing He can wake someone from. This hints at the Trinitarian shape of the Gospel, for the Son does what the Father does, John 5:19-21, and the raising of the dead is at once the Father's and the Son's work.

And He is a God who asks for trust before He gives understanding. 'Just believe,' to a man who has just heard that all is over, is a hard word. But it is spoken by the One who knows what He will do. The tension of the chapter is that God is both overwhelmingly strong and personally close, and the two are not at odds. The same hand that held back the sea takes a little girl's hand.

For worship, then, we praise a God whose power is not frightening to the needy but a refuge, whose holiness reaches out, who knows each by name and who is not stopped by death. The right response is the one the chapter models: to come, even trembling, to tell Him the whole truth, to go in peace, and to go home and tell what He has done.

crossReferences.note: The LORD holds out His hands to a people who sit among graves and eat pig's meat, a picture that fits the Gerasene man and his surroundings. In Mark 5 the one who was not seeking Him is sought, and what Isaiah described as a condition is met by a Person who crosses the sea.

Prisoners in chains and darkness cry out to the LORD and He breaks their chains and gates of bronze. The man in Mark 5, who had broken every chain and was still bound, is set free by a word. The psalm goes on, in verses 23 to 30, to the storm Jesus has just stilled.

The law of the woman with a long-lasting flow of blood, who was unclean as long as it lasted and made unclean anything she touched. This is the law that Mark 5:25-34 puts under pressure, since her touch does not defile Jesus but is met with healing.

Touching a corpse made a person unclean for seven days. When Jesus takes the dead girl by the hand in Mark 5:41, He does what the law marks out as defiling, and the result is that death is undone, not that He is made unclean.

Elijah stretches himself over the widow's dead son three times and prays, and the child lives. It is the closest precedent for Mark 5:41, and the contrast is instructive: where Elijah prays and strains, Jesus simply speaks and the girl rises.

Elisha raises the Shunammite's son by prayer and by lying on him, and the boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. This too stands behind Jairus' story, and Jesus' raising with a word shows Him to be more than a prophet.

God promises to sprinkle clean water on His people, cleanse them from their uncleanness, and give them a new heart and a new spirit. The cleansing that Jesus brings to the woman and the man in the tombs is a down payment on this promise.

Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake. The language of 'sleep' for the dead lies behind Jesus' words about the girl, and the verse shows that the Old Testament already holds out the hope of resurrection that Mark 5 illustrates.

Jesus raises the only son of a widow at Nain, touches the bier and says 'Young man, I say to you, get up.' It is a close parallel to Mark 5:41, showing that the raising of Jairus' daughter is part of a pattern of life-giving authority.

Lazarus is called out of the tomb after four days. It is the larger sign of the same power, and Jesus' words about Lazarus sleeping in John 11:11-14 echo His words about the girl being asleep in Mark 5:39.

Paul tells believers not to grieve like those without hope for those who 'have fallen asleep,' since God will bring them with Jesus. The calling of death a sleep, learned from Jesus' words in Mark 5:39, becomes part of the church's language of hope.

study.oneStory:
The story begins in Eden with a good creation in which God's people were not afraid of anything. The fall brought in the powers that Mark 5 shows at work: unclean spirits that enslave, sickness that wastes, and death that ends. These are the three great consequences of the curse, and this chapter shows Jesus overturning each in turn. The man in the tombs, the woman dried up for twelve years and the girl at twelve are the human faces of Genesis 3.

The chapter also fits the story of Israel. God had promised to redeem His people from the powers that held them, and Israel's rescue at the Red Sea was the pattern. The prophets looked for a deeper deliverance, from chains, from impurity and from the grave, as in Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, Ezekiel 37:12-14, where God says 'I will open your graves and bring you up from them.' Mark 5 shows that promise beginning to be kept, a grave opened here and there as signs of the great one still to come.

It looks beyond Israel too. The first person to proclaim Jesus in a Gentile region is a former demoniac, and it is the start of the movement that Genesis 12:3 anticipated, in which all the families of the earth are blessed. The unclean place becomes the first mission field.

It looks to the cross. The pigs are not the only things to drown: the cross is where Jesus bears the uncleanness He has been touching, and it is where the strong man's last hold is broken. His taking of a dead child's hand will become His own entering of death and coming out of it. The word He speaks to the girl is the word the angel will speak at the tomb.

And it ends in the new creation. In Revelation 21:4 God wipes away every tear, and death, mourning, crying and pain are no more. The woman who had suffered for twelve years has no more scourge, the man once pushed out of town sits among the people of God, and the girl whom Jesus lifted by the hand is only the first of a great number who will 'get up.' The sea that threatened the disciples is gone, Revelation 21:1, the tombs are empty, and nothing unclean can enter the city, Revelation 21:27, because everything in it has been made clean.

quiz.q: What does the deliverance of the Gerasene demoniac reveal about Jesus?

options.text: That He is Lord over even a legion of demons, freeing the most hopelessly enslaved with a word.
options.note: The many demons flee at His command and the man is restored, clothed and sane, Mark 5:8-15.

options.text: That He cares about people tormented by evil.
options.note: True, but the scene's main revelation is His sovereign authority over the whole host of demons.

options.text: That demons are stronger than most people realize.
options.note: The demons are strong, but the point is their utter powerlessness before Jesus, not their strength.

options.text: That Jesus needed the pigs to defeat the demons.
options.note: Jesus commands the demons directly; the pigs only display that the deliverance was real.

quiz.q: What actually healed the woman who touched Jesus' cloak?

options.text: Her faith laying hold of Jesus, who says her faith has healed her.
options.note: Mark 5:34; Jesus credits her faith, not the fabric, distinguishing her from the crowd merely pressing in.

options.text: Touching the special cloth of Jesus' garment.
options.note: She did touch His cloak, but Jesus makes clear it was her faith in Him, not magic in the cloth, that healed her.

options.text: The sheer press of the crowd around Jesus.
options.note: Many pressed against Him; only her believing touch drew healing power.

options.text: The skill of the many physicians she had seen.
options.note: The physicians had failed for twelve years; her healing came through faith in Jesus.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say to Jairus when news comes that his daughter has died?

options.text: Do not be afraid; just believe.
options.note: Mark 5:36 sets faith against fear even in the face of death.

options.text: It is too late now; nothing more can be done.
options.note: The opposite of Jesus' words; He calls Jairus to keep believing.

options.text: Your faith alone will raise her without My help.
options.note: It is Jesus who raises her; Jairus is called to trust Him, not to trust his own faith as a power.

options.text: Bring her to the synagogue for prayer.
options.note: Jesus does go to the house and act, but His actual word to Jairus is do not fear, just believe.

quiz.q: What is striking about Jesus touching the demoniac, the bleeding woman, and the dead girl?

options.text: He contacts what the law counted unclean, yet is not defiled; instead His holiness and life make them whole.
options.note: Jesus reverses the flow of defilement, cleansing and raising rather than being contaminated.

options.text: He was willing to help people others avoided.
options.note: True, but it misses the deeper point that His touch overcomes uncleanness itself.

options.text: He broke the law of Moses by touching them.
options.note: Rather than being defiled, Jesus overcomes the uncleanness; He is not shown as a lawbreaker but as the greater holiness.

options.text: It shows uncleanness was never a real concern in Israel.
options.note: Uncleanness was a serious barrier; the wonder is that Jesus reverses it.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus tell the freed demoniac to go home and tell what the Lord had done?

options.text: To send him as a witness to God's mercy among his own people in the Decapolis.
options.note: Mark 5:19-20; the restored man proclaims Jesus throughout the Gentile Decapolis.

options.text: Because the man wanted to stay with Jesus but was told to serve at home.
options.note: True that the man wished to follow, but the point is his commission to bear witness to God's mercy.

options.text: To keep the miracle completely secret.
options.note: Here Jesus sends him to tell, not to hide it, unlike the secrecy He often urged in Jewish areas.

options.text: Because Jesus did not want the man near Him.
options.note: Jesus acted in love, giving him a mission, not rejecting him.

questions: The demoniac was beyond anyone's power to help, yet not beyond Jesus. What situation feels beyond hope to you, and what would it mean to bring it to Him?
The woman reached out in faith amid a crowd that only pressed against Jesus. What is the difference between crowding near Jesus and truly touching Him by faith?
Jesus stopped to know and honour the trembling woman personally. How does it comfort you that Jesus wants not just to fix you but to know you?
To Jairus, Jesus said, do not be afraid, just believe. Where is fear crowding out faith in your life, even to the point where a situation feels as final as death?
The freed man was sent to tell his own people how much the Lord had done for him. What has the Lord done for you that your family and neighbours most need to hear?

translationNotes.note: The region is variously named Gerasenes, Gadarenes, or Gergesenes in the manuscripts, referring to the same Gentile district on the eastern shore of the lake; the difference does not affect the account.

Your faith has healed you translates a verb that also means has saved you, tying the bodily healing to the salvation faith receives; Jesus adds the warm address, Daughter, and the blessing, go in peace.

Talitha koum is Aramaic, the everyday language Jesus spoke; Mark preserves the actual words and then translates them, little girl, get up, showing the tender authority with which He addresses the dead child.
